**Altruism and self-interest** — whether and how action can aim at another's good rather than one's own — psychological egoism and its rivals, the empathy–altruism debate and self–other merging, inclusion of others in the self and identity fusion, team reasoning and group-directed preferences, identity in the utility function, the evolution of unselfish behaviour (kin, reciprocal and group selection), and the extent of the self as it bears on what counts as self-interest (ADR-062).

| [LIT-497](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-497.md) v2 | The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour. I | Hamilton (1964), J. Theor. Biol. 7:1–16. A one-locus model in which an individual's genotype affects relatives' fitness. Weighting each effect by Wright's coefficient of relationship r gives "inclusive fitness", which tends to be maximized as classical fitness is. An action that costs the actor is favoured only if the benefit to a relative exceeds 1/r times the cost: more than two brothers, four half-brothers or eight first cousins (§5). The increase of mean inclusive fitness is proved only for giving traits; the model is not about morality. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-401](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-401.md)); worth reading as the source of inclusive fitness and of the rule the moral-psychology literature calls Hamilton's rule. It is a population-genetic model with non-overlapping generations, random mating and weak selection, and its rule appears as −k > 1/r (§5), not in the later rb > c form. It proves that mean inclusive fitness increases only for genes whose total effect on others is non-negative (giving traits); for harming traits it shows only that selection points uphill. It says nothing about morality: it is the kin domain of morality-as-cooperation in its biological form, read as biology. |

| [LIT-1698](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1698.md) | Team Reasoning and Intentional Cooperation for Mutual Benefit | Sugden (2015). Social preferences cannot represent trust: on Rabin-style intention-based preferences, the common-knowledge practice of trust in the Trust Game is not an equilibrium. Team reasoning can, but not Bacharach's version, which maximizes a team utility, trades members' interests off against each other and needs no assurance that others reason as a team. Sugden's Schema of Cooperative Team Reasoning aims at each member's benefit over a maximin benchmark, follows existing practices and binds only given reciprocal reason to believe the others endorse it. So a market exchange that serves each party's interest can still be intended as mutual benefit, neither self-interest nor sacrifice. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1288](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1288.md)) from the published version, open under CC BY-NC-ND at the Journal of Social Ontology; worth reading as Sugden's own later statement of team reasoning, read in place of his 2003 paper ([LIT-1782](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1782.md), Unavailable), and for its claim that team reasoning cannot be reduced to self-interest or to social preferences by redefining payoffs, which bears on the owner's thesis ([CLAIM-491](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-491.md)). |

| [LIT-1703](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1703.md) | Culture and the self: Implications for cognition, emotion, and motivation | Markus & Kitayama (1991). A theoretical review. Cultures differ in how they construe the self. The independent construal, most clearly American and western European, is a bounded self defined by internal attributes. The interdependent construal, found in Japan and other Asian cultures but also in African, Latin American, Hindu and southern European ones, is a self defined by relationships with specific others in specific contexts: "others are included within the boundaries of the self" (p. 245), though it "does not result in a merging of self and other" (p. 228). The authors predict, and review evidence, that interdependent selves know more about others and describe themselves by context. They expect them to feel and express "other-focused" emotions (shame, sympathy, amae) more and "ego-focused" ones (anger, pride) less. They expect them to pursue achievement for others and to show modesty, not self-enhancement. They name a third option between selfishness and selflessness: "a self defined in relationship to others" (p. 247). | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1275](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1275.md)) from the published APA scan posted by Markus on her own website (hazelmarkus.com/research); worth reading as the classic statement that cultures construe the self as more or less inclusive of others. It does not support the step to self-interest: the authors deny merging and allow "genuine, other-oriented, altruistic" motives. The evidence is mostly cross-national contrasts, often second-hand or unpublished, with culture standing in for an unmeasured construal. |

| [LIT-1729](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1729.md) | Empirical Approaches to Altruism | The SEP survey of the empirical egoism–altruism debate, revised in 2025. On the standard account, altruism needs an ultimate desire for another's well-being; biological and social-science senses of "altruism" settle nothing about it. Self-other merging is a different challenge: only numerical identity with the helped person would make helping egoistic, and none of the four measures used by Cialdini et al. and Batson et al. | [LIT-1752](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1752.md) | Economics and Identity | Akerlof & Kranton (2000). Adds identity, "a person's sense of self", to the utility function: U = U(own actions, others' actions, I), where I depends on one's assigned social categories, how well one's own traits match the category's ideal, and how far one's own and others' actions follow the category's prescriptions. Violating one's prescriptions costs utility (Is); others' violations cost it too (Io), and the loser may pay to "respond", harming the violator. A two-person game shows when such responses deter. Applied to occupational segregation by sex, to "oppositional" identities chosen by the socially excluded, and to wives who earn more yet still do most of the housework, it yields predictions standard models do not. Evidence is illustrative: ethnographies, a 70-household vignette survey, census shares and a Panel Study of Income Dynamics regression. Identity is modelled as self-image to be maintained, not as concern for a group's welfare. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1311](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1311.md)) from the journal's typeset text deposited in Duke University's repository DukeSpace (hdl.handle.net/10161/1993; Unpaywall labels it the submitted version, but it carries the journal's pagination and copyright line), fetched through the repository's own API; worth reading as the founding statement of identity economics: identity as self-image in the utility function, with prescriptions and identity externalities, applied to gender at work, exclusion and the household. Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Sugden 2015 ([LIT-1698](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1698.md)). |
| [LIT-1783](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1783.md) | Empathy, Altruism, and Group Identification | A conceptual paper. It takes Cialdini et al.'s claim that empathy-induced helping is due to self-other merging and asks what "merging" could coherently mean. May argued that every reading either attributes absurd beliefs or fails to explain helping. The authors answer that merging is group identification: in empathizing with Y, X comes to conceive of Y as part of X's social self, so Y's welfare becomes constitutive of "our" welfare. They argue that this reading is behaviourally adequate, because it explains Batson's results in the same way as minimal-group favouritism, and psychologically plausible, because it posits a non-doxastic self-representation rather than a belief in being two bodies. Helping so motivated is then altruistic at the individual level and egoistic at the group level. The empirical dispute with Batson et al. (1997) is set aside. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1277](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1277.md)), in place of [LIT-1728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1728.md) and [LIT-1700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1700.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the only work in the record that states the owner's thesis for empathic helping in a precise form: concern for another's welfare is non-instrumental, and that welfare is constitutive of the helper's first-person plural welfare. It offers no measure of group identification apart from empathy. |
